title: Close three backend findings from the industry-standard review: wrong HTTP status codes, a timing-unsafe token comparison, and unlogged auth refusals

approvals.evidence: "You already have priority" (2026-09-06), in response to the assistant naming the remaining review findings, in descending severity, as the standing work queue after the security correction (ART-20260906-034) and the accessibility batch (ART-20260906-037/038).

body.problem: Six-dimension industry-standard review (2026-09-06) confirmed three backend findings, none HIGH but each a named standards gap: (1) app/api/mail/file/route.ts returned 200/no-explicit-status for what are really 404/409 conditions -- a dedupe conflict, a refused create, an issue-not-found, and a refused attach -- contrary to RFC 9110 status-code semantics and the Microsoft REST API Guidelines this codebase otherwise follows; (2) app/api/intake/route.ts compared the caller's bearer token to the configured shared secret with a plain !== string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and leaks how many leading characters matched through response timing (OWASP A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures) -- the one control standing between the open internet and a write on this specifically unauthenticated-by-design endpoint; (3) no route logged anything server-side when a request was refused for authentication (401) or authorization (403) reasons, across every write/mutate/read-sensitive endpoint that checks a session or a permission -- so repeated probing, credential stuffing, or a misconfigured client silently hammering a permission it does not hold, left no trace to alert on or correlate (OWASP A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures).

source.reference: Industry-standard review workflow (2026-09-06), six independent reviewers each citing a named external standard (OWASP Top 10 2021, RFC 9110, Prisma/Postgres conventions, React/Next.js conventions, WCAG 2.1 AA, NN/g heuristics), each finding adversarially verified by a separate agent before being reported. Version 2 additionally incorporates F1 from this batch's own independent pre-merge review (a general-purpose review agent, 2026-09-06): the intake endpoint's own bearer-token 401 had been scoped out of logAuthRefusal on the reasoning that it has no session actor to log -- a mistake, since the helper's actor parameter is optional and this route is exactly the one control facing anonymous internet traffic, making its refusals the highest-value ones to log in this whole batch.

scope_in: app/api/mail/file/route.ts: dedupe-conflict, create-refused, issue-not-found and attach-refused responses return 409/409/404/409 respectively instead of 200 or an implicit 200

app/api/intake/route.ts: the bearer-token comparison against the configured shared secret uses node:crypto's timingSafeEqual with a length check first, mirroring the existing pattern in lib/auth/seal.ts

lib/authLog.ts (new): a single logAuthRefusal(route, reason, actor) helper that writes one console.warn line per refusal, matching the one refusal this codebase already logs (app/api/auth/callback/route.ts's sign-in-failed warning)

logAuthRefusal wired into every 401/403 refusal site across app/api/mail/file/route.ts, app/api/workspace/route.ts, app/api/mail/send/route.ts, app/api/documents/route.ts and app/api/documents/[id]/route.ts (13 sites in total)
app/api/intake/route.ts's own bearer-token-mismatch 401 also calls logAuthRefusal, with no actor (the caller is anonymous) -- added in v2, see source above
scope_out: app/api/mail/file/route.ts's 'reconnect your inbox' 401 -- a benign onboarding-incomplete state (the person has not yet linked a mailbox), not a security-relevant refusal, so logging it would be noise rather than signal. Confirmed still the right call in v2's own pre-merge review (rated LOW, not MEDIUM, precisely because the caller there is already an authenticated session rather than anonymous traffic)

The remaining findings from the same review: importWorkspace batching (lib/db/repo.ts), the missing HierarchyNode.sowId index (requires a Prisma migration and architect approval), the HIGH migration expand/contract policy finding (a documentation/process decision, not a code fix), and the remaining frontend findings in components/IssueWorkspace.tsx -- separate corrections

acceptance_criteria.given: a mail already filed against an issue (matching internetMessageId)
acceptance_criteria.when: the same message is filed again

acceptance_criteria.given: a create-mode file-mail request whose persistActions call is refused by the reducer
an attach-mode file-mail request naming an issue id that does not exist or is soft-deleted
an attach-mode file-mail request whose persistActions call is refused by the reducer
the existing UI caller of this endpoint (components/InboxPanel.tsx)
acceptance_criteria.when: any of the above responses is returned
acceptance_criteria.then: the caller's existing behaviour is unchanged, because it reads the parsed JSON body's ok field and never inspects res.ok or the HTTP status

acceptance_criteria.given: a bearer token presented to /api/intake that differs from the configured secret by one byte at any position, including the last
acceptance_criteria.then: no observable timing difference correlates with which byte differs, because the comparison is a constant-time equality check rather than a short-circuiting one

acceptance_criteria.given: any of the 13 named 401/403 refusal sites across the five session-based route files
acceptance_criteria.then: exactly one console.warn line is emitted naming the route, the actor (or 'unresolved actor' when none is known), and the refusal reason, before the HTTP response is returned

acceptance_criteria.given: the logged reason and route strings
acceptance_criteria.then: they contain no token, password, session cookie, or full request body -- only the route path, a short human-readable refusal reason already safe to show the caller, and the actor's own id/name

acceptance_criteria.given: a request to /api/intake whose bearer token does not match the configured secret
acceptance_criteria.then: exactly one console.warn line is emitted naming the route and 'bearer token mismatch', with no actor (the caller is anonymous)

business_rules: BR1 (E1, this review). A response describing a resource conflict, a not-found condition, or a refused write must carry the matching HTTP status code (RFC 9110); a 200 with an ok:false body is not a substitute where a caller or an intermediary (proxy, monitoring, cache) reasonably keys behaviour off status.

BR2 (E1, this review). A secret comparison reachable from an untrusted caller must run in constant time with respect to the secret's content; length may be checked first only because timingSafeEqual itself requires equal-length buffers, not as a substitute for the content comparison being constant-time.

BR3 (E1, this review). Every authentication or authorization refusal must produce one server-side log line naming the route, the actor when one is known, and the reason -- an absent session actor is a reason to log with no actor, not a reason to skip logging, and is the more urgent case on a route facing unauthenticated traffic.
